html:
The founding of Gadir, today's Cádiz in southwest Spain, by Phoenician traders from Tyre, beyond the Strait of Gibraltar on the Atlantic coast. It is one of the oldest cities in western Europe.

Ancient writers gave a date around 1100 BCE. Archaeology so far points to the 9th or 8th century BCE. Either way, Gadir was among the farthest outposts of the Phoenician cities, some 3,500 kilometres from home.

The draw was silver. Inland lay the land the Greeks called Tartessos, rich in silver and other metals from the mines of the Rio Tinto region. The Phoenicians traded oil, wine and fine goods for metal, which they shipped east to the Levant and, in time, to the Assyrian empire that demanded tribute from Tyre. Gadir also fished and salted tuna.

Its temple of the god Melqart, whom the Greeks took for Heracles, was famous throughout the ancient world. Gadir later came under Carthage and then Rome, and became a rich Roman city.
